title: Maple and the Lost Griffon
markdown:
Elf Eben’s house sat high enough that clouds sometimes queued at the chimney. His garden clung to the slope, a quilt of herbs and stubborn colour, each bed labelled in a hand so neat it looked like a poem that had decided to grow. He whispered to plants as if they were shy guests. Moonpetal got mist from a sphere of captured light and a suggested drop of evening dew. His voice was rustling leaves on purpose.

Maple uncurled from the warm stone, reddish-brown, tail already conducting an orchestra nobody had hired, a furry exclamation in his calm. She had opinions about beetles, paths, and the correct number of surprises in a morning. “A bit more sunlight? Or a tickle behind the ears? Or a fun chase after something wriggly?”

“Beetles are for watching. And this moonpetal is being bothered.”

He knelt until his neat knees met soil. Near the moonpetals, where only his own soft boot prints should have signed the earth, other marks: too small for a grown traveller, too big for a squirrel’s punctuation, round, a little splayed at the front, as if the visitor had been unsure of landing. “Someone has called without writing first.”

Maple’s whiskers worked. “Not us. Old. Sunshine on warm rock after rain. A smell that has been waiting.”

Elder Willow shuffled from the path she always took, face lined like bark, keeper of rites the village remembered only when something odd turned up in a respectable garden. She peered, sharp as winter. “Ah. Time for the Rite of the First Bloom.”

“Does it involve a field guide?”

Pebble-chuckle. “Offering. A pattern. Then the mountain tells.”

“Facing the sunrise three times at dusk,” Eben murmured. “I shall adjust my clock.”

Maple’s tail voted yes. Smells! They went, satchel adjusted, Maple already a red thread through trees. He let her lead the unnoticed path—a tip learned the hard way, after a root and a dignity incident. Foxes find the doors forests keep for themselves. Sunlight dappled moss. She stopped, barked a footnote, wriggled a fern curtain, glanced back to make sure the elf had not become a statue of caution. He stepped over the root she had leapt. “Always the fox,” he told himself, dry, fond.

A ledge opened and the mountain had, apparently, thrown a party: market like a carpet of banners, red yellow blue snapping, merchants with lungs, honey and roasted nuts, laughter like small bells. Eben, who loved order, stood amazed in the useful way, the way a tidy person admits a mess can be a kind of music. Maple’s soul left her body for a stall of dried berries, particularly a plump bunch that deserved a sonnet. A playful gust tugged cloak and fur; tiny stones clattered downhill, cheerful as gossip. They laughed. Then her nose changed key. Not party. Worry. Loneliness, old-sunshine still, but thinner.

Prints ran to a moss-hidden cave. A faint sad sound. “Small,” Maple said. “Like a lost button.”

Willow arrived, herbs, out of breath. “The Rite before sunset. East, three times.”

“A bit much for a lost creature.”

She was already chanting order into the dark. Eben followed; Maple stayed close. Cool stone. In the deepest shadow: a griffon chick, messy down, drooping beak, golden eyes full of fear. The ancient words, meant as comfort, arrived as weather. It peeped, retreated, a frightened comma.

“We made it worse.”

“More rock parsley,” Willow suggested.

The cave felt colder. Sad chirps came from a distance that was only a few yards and also a country. Eben sat on rough ground that was not his garden, heels and helplessness. Hands good at coaxing petals felt unemployed. He had come for a pattern, a who and a how, and found a pulse that flinched at Latin-sounding comfort.

Maple sensed the quiet worry the way she sensed beetles: accurately, without a field guide. She padded into the dim without rush, sat a little off, and hummed—a hearth-purr, a fire that had decided not to show off. She nudged a loose stone, looked back, tail a slow promise. Her usual wild-mountain scent went gentle, hearth-steady. Not a threat. Understanding, offered like a bowl.

A small feathered head peeked. Wide gold. Beak opening on silence. Maple sighed kindness, then a tiny yip of here, of not-alone. Wobbly step, another. Sniff. Speed, surprising, toward the hum. Beak to nose: a bridge you could miss if you were chanting. She licked the downy head, nudged toward the mouth of the cave, toward Eben and the ordinary mercy of daylight.

Willow’s chant had stopped. “Not herbs. Comfort. A friend who smells of home.” Respect, new, for a fox.

As if Maple’s hum had posted a letter the sky could read, a parent griffon stooped from the late sun, wings a majesty that made the ledge feel briefly borrowed. Shadow, a deep call that was not a rite and needed none. The chick ran. Flurry of chirps and nuzzles, the silent paperwork of families. Then a beat, and twilight took two shapes instead of one frightened one.

Willow watched them go with her unused parsley still fragrant. Eben’s smile was uncatalogued. Maple shook as if the day had been a stroll and a berry stall and nothing more dramatic than wind. He did not say the grandest adventure was friendship. He said, quieter, that he had hunted who and how and missed why, and that a cave is a poor place for a field guide. She thumped the rock. “Lost. Needed a friend. You are a good one. I am also a good one.” A leap, small, allowed.

Garden again. Moonpetals opened silver mirrors. The prints had gone with the breeze. Eben knelt to be, not to mend. Maple’s breath kept time. The quiet that returned had a chick-shaped space in it, which was, he found, an acceptable kind of untidy.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
